Here's the thing:

Naming your child can be also extremely harmful as well. Name your child something that is unique (and appears to be hard to pronounce...without offending someone) will hurt their chances at gainful employment.

Take a stack of 30 resumes, 29 are commonly used names and 1 looks difficult to say without making a mistake, the single resume is possibly getting skipped. It doesn't have anything to do with nationalism, sexism, racism, or your sexual orientation. People just don't like fucking up and having to apologize. Why bother if they already have 29 other applicants?

I'm in a very multicultural city, so if people here were that afraid of mispronouncing a name on the phone, business would pretty much grind to a halt!

Anyway, I don't think most grownups are that afraid of at least trying to say a hard name. Worst case, you get it wrong and the person corrects you, and then you know how to say it. Big deal. And that person is probably used to correcting how people say their name, anyway (I know I am!), so they're not going to get offended unless they're some kind of nutbar, in which case... no interview for that applicant!

I would say the thing that might get someone's resume passed over here is a joke name, like North West. Would a high-powered investment firm, for example, take a resume with that name on it seriously? You have to wonder.

As for difficult-to-pronounce unusual names, I feel like mine (it's not Pandora, of course) has given me an advantage sometimes. I'm pretty sure that when I've been job hunting, some of the interviews I got were because my name made people curious and they wanted to see who I was. My name doesn't immediately conjure up a specific "type" of person in people's minds, I don't think.
